By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 27, 2026 at 1:17PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than AbbVie ›.

Over the past five years, AbbVie (ABBV -0.88%) has more than tripled the S&P 500's total return, despite losing patent exclusivity for its biggest growth driver, Humira, an immunology medicine. The firm's ability to overcome the loss of Humira, the best-selling drug in the industry's history, speaks volumes about its underlying business. But where might AbbVie be headed over the next five years? Let's see whether the drugmaker can continue beating the market.

AbbVie's core growth drivers in recent years have been Skyrizi and Rinvoq, two immunology drugs that have earned numerous indications overlapping with those of Humira. In fact, these two drugs have demonstrated superior efficacy compared to Humira across several indications. For instance, in a Phase 3 study in certain patients with plaque psoriasis, AbbVie pitted Skyrizi against Humira, and the former performed better.

In a recent development, rinvoq also beat Humira in studies in some patients with rheumatoid arthritis. It's no wonder, then, that these two medicines already combine to generate more than Humira's $21.2 billion peak annual sales. Through Sept. 30, Skyrizi's revenue was $15.8 billion, up 25.6% year over year. Rinvoq's sales came in at $7.4 billion, 23.9% higher than the year-ago period. What's more, both have secured several expansions this year and should win more over the next five years.

Industry observers note that and neither will lose patent exclusivity until at least 2033. Note that they have made it a habit to exceed expectations. AbbVie expects them to combine for more than $31 billion in sales this year. It had initially set a $31 billion combined target for 2027 (and even that 2027 guidance was $4 billion above a previous one).

True, the competitive landscape will evolve over the next few years. That could be a problem for AbbVie. But even with that caveat, we can expect Skyrizi and Rinvoq to continue performing well over the medium term.

NYSE · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

It has been revealed that five years is enough time for AbbVie to launch several upcoming products that will help it improve its financial results and overcome challenges, including government-led drug price negotiations in the U.S., which could reduce sales for some of its products. The pharmaceutical leader boasts several promising candidates investors should keep an eye on. One of the most promising is zumilokibart, an investigational medicine for eczema. Here's why this candidate looks particularly attractive.

Sources indicate that according to some estimates, the eczema drug market was valued at $21 billion last year and could rise to $46 billion by 2034. It's a highly competitive industry, but zumilokibart has shown promising efficacy data while also benefiting from a very convenient twice-a-year maintenance dosing schedule, something no currently approved medicine in the U.S. offers.

If zumilokibart performs well in Phase 3 studies and earns approval within the next five years, it could help strengthen AbbVie's portfolio and extend its lead in immunology. Another important candidate AbbVie is working on is ABBV-295, an investigational weight-loss medicine, perhaps one of the fastest-growing therapeutic areas in the industry.

AbbVie licensed ABBV-295 from a Denmark-based organization. The weight loss drug market might be worth $150 billion by 2035, up from $15 billion in 2024. AbbVie's ABBV-295 is being investigated as a long-acting treatment and, if approved, may be administered once per month. Investors should also keep track of ABBV-295's progress over the next few years, and these two candidates are only the tip of the iceberg. AbbVie is developing many more brand-newly introduced drugs and could have an even stronger portfolio by 2031.

In the meantime, the firm expects no major loss of patent exclusivity through the end of the decade.

The market is well aware of AbbVie's excellent prospects. That's why the drugmaker's shares have crushed broader equities this year. But is the stock too expensive? Not in my view. AbbVie is at the moment trading at 18.5x forward earnings, versus an average of 19.2x for healthcare stocks. One might argue that AbbVie is worth a premium over its peers, especially those in the pharmaceutical industry. Many drugmakers will face major patent cliffs by 2030, and few post sales and earnings growth as consistently as AbbVie's.

In a recent development, further, AbbVie has an outstanding dividend program, having increased its payouts for 55 consecutive years, making it a Dividend King (a company with 50 or more consecutive dividend increases). Given all that, I'd value AbbVie slightly above 20x forward earnings. So, at current levels, the stock looks like a steal.

Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some upcoming money goals and make progress toward them.
  • That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.
  • “You’re probably not doing too much,” states Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some upcoming money goals and make progress toward them.

That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

“You’re probably not doing too much,” states Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”.

One crucial component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

According to recent reports, “We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”.

According to recent reports, ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

Industry observers note that what’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

“Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird indicates. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”.

Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman claims.

If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the fresh saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

Once you’ve outlined those massive goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird states.

He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he notes.

Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird states.

“Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he notes. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”.

Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

Industry observers note that with credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird notes. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.).

“High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman says. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

In a recent development, even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

“It’s like a diet,” Baird notes. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”.

In a recent development, “Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

Sources indicate that in fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he indicates. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”.

History notes some of the best opportunities to invest in technology companies have come several months after their much-anticipated IPOs.

Industry observers note that according to Equity Comp Academy, citing research from Nasdaq (NDAQ +1.93%), more than 70% of technology stocks underperform after going public. And some of the biggest tech IPOs of 2026 have been particularly disappointing for investors who bought shares on the first day of trading.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS +5.08%) went public in May at $185 per share and closed its first day of trading at $311. Anyone who bought Cerebras stock at that price was sitting on a nearly 65% loss by the end of October, when shares traded at roughly $110.

Sources indicate that and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +4.83%) stock went from an IPO price of $135 in June to nearly $161 at the end of its first day of trading. But SpaceX shares are now about $127.

Recent findings suggest that you can find similar examples going back several years. What's particularly interesting is how little time investors often had to wait to get those stocks at a discount to their IPO prices.

Data source: Author research, public Nasdaq data.

Sources indicate that I also wouldn't get too hung up on the IPO price when deciding when to buy a stock. Investors who bought Cerebras stock at $185 after watching it soar to $311 may have thought they were getting a bargain. But they still could have saved themselves a lot of money by waiting.

Perhaps my favorite example is Meta Platforms (META +3.13%), which went public as Facebook in 2012 at $38 per share. The stock fell below its IPO price on its second day of trading and didn't get back to that level for 14 months.

Meta has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. Investors certainly didn't need to buy Facebook stock in May 2012 to become wealthy from owning it.

Established technology companies have years of quarterly earnings reports for investors to review, assessing how well management has met its projections and how Wall Street has valued the stock relative to its earnings or revenue.

Sources indicate that but that's not the case with Anthropic -- or any big tech IPO. So it's no surprise that those companies see significant volatility in the first few days. Before I invest in Anthropic, I want more detail about how much it spends on computing infrastructure. Anthropic can have outstanding revenue growth and still be years away from generating the kind of profits that justify its valuation.

NASDAQ · As of 1:15 PM ET 11/27/26.

Am I risking paying more for Anthropic stock six months from now? Sure. Arm Holdings (ARM +6.22%) and Airbnb (ABNB +4.07%) both more than doubled in value in their first year as publicly traded companies, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

But I'd rather pay a little more for Anthropic stock after seeing a couple of quarterly earnings reports if those numbers give me greater conviction in the firm's ability to make money.

Plenty of people have made fortunes investing in technology stocks without ever participating in an IPO. In the long run, buying based on business fundamentals rather than debut-day hype is the far more reliable path to wealth -- and I don't see why investing in Anthropic should be any different.

What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the firm's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
  • Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the manufacturer.
  • Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the firm's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the manufacturer. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider noted in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

Sources indicate that it's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The organization had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

It has been revealed that coreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, mentioned CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person.".

Industry observers note that "There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he stated in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us.".

According to recent reports, bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any major changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real problem is just how much money the manufacturer will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

In a recent development, "Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies.".

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

Recent findings suggest that burry isn't done with semiconductor stocks, either. He sold most of his bearish put options on Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%) as the stock fell this month, while saying his original thesis "still has legs." His plan, he wrote, is to bet against Nvidia again "nearer $200/share during a period of market optimism. That time is not now." Nvidia closed Friday at $150.49.

Chinese stocks also carry risks U.S. stocks don't, including shifting government policy, U.S.-China trade fights, and accounting rules that give investors less visibility. JD's low valuation partly reflects those risks, along with fierce price competition in Chinese e-commerce.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Burry can change course in days, and he often does, but the core idea is worth borrowing. When a profitable market leader trades at a record-low valuation because of fear rather than collapsing fundamentals, patient investors can be paid for waiting. If you want exposure to e-commerce stocks in China, JD is a reasonable place to start, as a small position you're prepared to hold for years. Investors who'd rather avoid China-specific risk can apply the same lesson at home: build a watch list of quality tech stocks that have been knocked down, and buy in stages.

4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (752 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
  • Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
  • According to recent reports, but what about your money?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

According to recent reports, but what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

According to recent reports, last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

It has been revealed that if systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, mentioned Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good blueprint, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

Sources indicate that “My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson mentioned. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

Industry observers note that if your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge states. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

In a recent development, if you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

Sources indicate that make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

Industry observers note that and set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the massive concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he states. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” noted Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.

NYSE · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

In a recent development, since peaking in late May, shares of the space and defense stock have shed 74% of their value to just $6 and change. That's well below the $10 per share Redwire cost at the time of its 2021 SPAC IPO.

Although free cash flow-negative and unprofitable (analysts polled by S&P Global Market Intelligence don't expect to see GAAP profits before 2029), Redwire trades below what I consider a fair valuation for unprofitable space stocks at just 3.1x trailing sales.

Industry News: BigBear.ai vs. Cerebras Systems: Which Artificial Intelligence Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 1:51PM EST.
  • The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has created a divide between software providers and hardware infrastructure giants.
  • Industry observers note that bigBear.ai focuses on decision AI for defense and intelligence agencies, while Cerebras Systems builds massive wafer-scale processors to accelerate artificial intelligence model training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 1:51PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than BigBear.ai ›.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence has created a divide between software providers and hardware infrastructure giants. Choosing between BigBear.ai (BBAI +6.92%) and Cerebras Systems (CBRS +5.08%) requires weighing government contracts against massive computing power.

Industry observers note that bigBear.ai focuses on decision AI for defense and intelligence agencies, while Cerebras Systems builds massive wafer-scale processors to accelerate artificial intelligence model training. These companies represent two distinct paths into the growing AI market, offering investors a choice between specialized software and high-performance hardware.

In a recent development, bigBear.ai focuses on AI-powered decision intelligence software, positioning itself as a unique player among tech stocks serving the defense industry. It uses a land and expand strategy by deploying minimally viable products to evaluate the potential for long-term government contracts. Because it derives significant revenue from a limited number of defense and intelligence agencies, customer concentration adds a layer of risk to the business.

It has been revealed that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $142.1 million, reflecting a decrease of roughly 1.5% compared to the prior year. The firm reported a net loss of $180.2 million during this period. This performance highlights the challenges of scaling software services within the rigid budgetary cycles of government clients.

It has been revealed that as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was zero, indicating a very low level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, which measures a organization's ability to cover short-term debts with assets that can be converted to cash within a year, was 1.8x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $46.3 million.

Industry observers note that cerebras Systems builds massive semiconductor infrastructure, including wafer-scale systems designed to train large-scale AI models more efficiently than traditional chips. Its systems are used by organizations in medical research, cryptography, and energy, while its infrastructure is deployed in data centers worldwide. This specialized focus helps the manufacturer target niche markets that require high-density computing power.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $755.8 million, which represents growth of 79.9% over the previous twelve-month period. Despite this rapid top-line expansion, the company reported a net loss of $651.4 million. The significant growth illustrates the high demand for specialized AI hardware as developers race to build more complex models.

According to recent reports, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the tech giant had a debt-to-equity ratio of -0.5x, which indicates that total liabilities exceed shareholder equity. The current ratio was 2.1x, suggesting a solid ability to meet short-term financial obligations. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was negative $392.8 million.

BigBear.ai faces substantial revenue concentration since a few government customers provide most of its funding, making it vulnerable to budget shifts or contract terminations. The tech giant has also navigated operational hurdles, including a $76.7 million goodwill impairment in late 2026 and legal challenges related to historical accounting restatements. Furthermore, it depends on third-party cloud infrastructure from providers like Microsoft (MSFT +0.60%) and Amazon (AMZN +3.96%), to deliver its software.

Cerebras operates in a highly capital-intensive industry where it must compete against established giants and rapidly evolving technology standards. The company is at the moment reporting significant net losses and negative cash flow as it invests heavily in its unique wafer-scale technology. Because it seeks to disrupt a market dominated by massive competitors, any delays in manufacturing or shifts in AI architecture could threaten its market share.

BigBear.ai appears to be the more conservatively priced option because it carries a much lower P/S ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Recent findings suggest that between BigBear.ai or Cerebras Systems for exposure to the artificial intelligence market, I would pick Cerebras. The organization's proprietary semiconductor chip technology enables AI systems to operate at faster speeds than those offered by larger competitors. This contributed to Cerebras gaining AI tech giants OpenAI, Microsoft, and Oracle as customers.

Meanwhile, BigBear.ai saw sales sink in 2025 after the U.S. government performed budget cuts. The company's revenue is rebounding in 2026, with full-year sales forecasted to come in between $150 million to $165 million, up from 2025's $127.7 million. However, the fact that the federal government could cut funding to BigBear.ai last year suggests its technology is not critical.

Moreover, the software manufacturer's reliance on federal contracts keeps it exposed to sudden shifts to its top-line growth. Its stock's lower valuation reflects this vulnerability, and until BigBear.ai can expand outside government dependence, Cerebras' innovative chips provide a better path to a return on your investment despite its stock's higher valuation.

10 stocks we like better than GE Vernova ›.

It has been revealed that it's Black Friday, and millions of shoppers will hit stores and websites for the biggest retail day of the year. Meanwhile, Wall Street is quietly running a clearance sale of its own.

Industry observers note that warren Buffett famously loves a good sale. "Whether we're talking about socks or stocks, I like buying quality merchandise when it is marked down," he once wrote.

Recent findings suggest that the recent market sell-off has left plenty of high-quality businesses sitting on the clearance rack. We asked our analysts to name one stock they think is on sale right now, and why. Here's what they picked (as a reminder, these are personal views and not official Motley Fool recommendations, so be sure to do your own research before buying).

GE Vernova's (GEV +2.84%) business has rarely looked stronger, but its stock tells a different story. Artificial intelligence (AI) data centers require massive amounts of power, and the high-voltage transformers and gas turbines needed to deliver it are in short supply.

Industry observers note that that demand pushed GE Vernova's backlog to $197 billion in the third quarter of fiscal year 2026, providing multi-year revenue visibility. Until a few months ago, the company didn't expect backlog to hit $200 billion before 2028. Its turbine factory slots are getting sold out through 2032, and it has struck a deal to acquire Trench Group for $9 billion, vertically integrating to secure critical grid parts.

GE Vernova ended Q3 with nearly $17 billion in cash, generated $5.4 billion in free cash flow, and doubled its stock buyback proposal to $20 billion.

With the stock down nearly 32% over the past six months, I'd say this is one AI stock on sale you can't go wrong with.

Alphabet (GOOG +0.54%) (GOOGL +0.68%) stock has reached bargain-basement levels, trading around 21x forward earnings estimates, as investors worry about the company's hefty investment in the AI infrastructure build-out.

Industry observers note that that said, Alphabet's spending helps serve existing demand, and the cloud backlog of $561 billion suggests a huge wave of revenue growth lies ahead. On top of this, Google Search's longtime search market dominance should support ongoing ad revenue growth. Still, Alphabet's main risk is lasting pressure on free cash flow if the AI spending deepens and drags on.

It has been revealed that despite enduring a rocky ride, Amazon (AMZN +3.96%) investors continue to prosper, with the stock outpacing the broader S&P 500 so far this year. It's easy to see why.

E-commerce sales climbed nearly 12% year over year this far in 2026, while its industry-leading cloud revenue from Amazon Web Services (AWS) jumped 35% -- thanks to strong enterprise adoption of the manufacturer's artificial intelligence services. The company has become the world's third-largest digital advertiser, with ad sales up 20%.

Recent findings suggest that wall Street expects Amazon to grow its top line by nearly 16% annually over the next five years. Yet for all that growth, Amazon is remarkably cheap, selling for just 21 times earnings, well below its average three-year multiple of 39. That's a price worthy of Black Friday.

In a recent development, as of Nov. 19, Nu Holdings (NU +4.45%) is down 29% in 2026. Most of that drop came from one painful Brazilian election week. But political noise tends to be temporary, and this too shall pass.

I bought my first shares on Oct. 26, right after the stock fell 17% in a day on progressive-leaning election results.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, the stock trades at 11 times forward earnings while the business grew sales 37% last quarter. That's a wide-open buying window, and I climbed through it with an open wallet.

In a recent development, nu makes over $1 billion a quarter in bottom-line profit with a return on equity above 31%. It signed up 3.7 million new customers in Q3 alone. The manufacturer also just secured a banking license in Brazil with no extra capital strings attached. And there's the U.S. launch, with Visa alum Rob Livingston as the California-based CFO. Nu is no longer a one-country story (or even stricly a Latin American business), and innovation outlasts election cycles.

Recent findings suggest that lula gets another four years, and Brazilian borrowers are paying late more often. Brazilian politics and late-stage credit quality could keep Nu's stock bumpy for a while.

Quarterly revenue at Anthropic (ANT +10.98%) has grown twelvefold in a year to $17 billion. Wow. More remarkably, existing customers are spending 9X what they did a year earlier. Claude is evolving from a software subscription into a fundamental business resource. And Anthropic is approaching operating breakeven. Most of its reported net loss stems from non-cash accounting charges. With shares below their IPO price, investors are buying extraordinary enterprise customer demand at a discount to the long-term opportunity. This is a B2B juggernaut.

KLA (KLAC +4.96%) dominates the market for finding microscopic defects in semiconductor manufacturing. The more complex chips become, the more financially damaging each defect becomes. That makes KLA increasingly indispensable. Quarterly revenue rose 29%, while free cash flow reached $1.34 billion. Its growing population of installed machines also generates recurring service revenue. KLA benefits not merely from greater chip production but from the rising difficulty of making each chip. And 20-year CEO Richard Wallace, an unsung hero, is one of the best-performing leaders in technology.

According to recent reports, billionToOne (BLLN +2.38%) uses proprietary genetic technology to detect incredibly small amounts of DNA associated with pregnancy and cancer. Quarterly testing volume increased 25%, average selling prices rose 18%, and cancer revenue nearly doubled. Gross margins reached 71%, alongside positive operating profits and free cash flow. The December launch of a blood-only test for detecting residual cancer expands BLLN's opportunity. Unlike many young diagnostics companies, BillionToOne has demonstrated that scientific innovation can finance further scientific innovation. I expect this company to deliver top-line growth and rising returns on capital for a long time to come!I believe all three of these stocks will beat the market over the next five years and yet I also believe all three will be more volatile than the market.

Recent findings suggest that A lower price tag doesn't make a stock a bargain by default. As Buffett's quote reminds us, the key word is "quality" -- some stocks are marked down for a reason.

So before you buy, ask two questions: Why did the price drop, and would you still want to own this business at full price? If the answer is yes, the discount is just a bonus. If the answer is yes, the discount is a bonus.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.).

In a recent development, is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

Recent findings suggest that first, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout swiftly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

According to recent reports, zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three key forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:.

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

It has been revealed that the following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

According to recent reports, the major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One crucial clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

Recent findings suggest that from here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Philadelphia 76ers could be short-staffed when they take on the Indiana Pacers in NBA Cup play on Friday night.

According to recent reports, shooting guard Jaylen Brown has already been ruled out with a hamstring injury. Center Joel Embiid is listed as questionable due to a lingering illness that has sidelined him for Philadelphia's last two games.

According to recent reports, brown picked up the hamstring issue in Wednesday's NBA Cup win over the Miami Heat. He left the game late in the first half and did not return. The guard missed two games last week with a left hamstring strain, but returned to action against the Portland Trail Blazers and played 29 minutes.

Toward the end of the first half, the Philadelphia guard reached toward his left hamstring and shook his head before checking himself out of the game.

Sources indicate that embiid is dealing with an illness, though not much has been released about what symptoms he may be dealing with. Regardless, he has missed two consecutive games. The center was listed as questionable for Wednesday's game against the Heat, but was downgraded before the game.

In a recent development, with no Embiid and no Brown for a half, LeBron James and Tyrese Maxey took over and led the 76ers to a win over the Heat on Wednesday. James logged his first triple-double as a 76er with 25 points, 10 rebounds and 12 assists. Maxey added 30 points, 4 rebounds and 6 assists.

The win moved Philadelphia to 15-4. Friday's game against Indiana is the front end of a back-to-back, and a win would help the 76ers clinch their NBA Cup group.

By Eric Volkman – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:01PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than RTX ›.

In a recent development, storied defense company RTX (RTX +1.17%) notched a win just before Thanksgiving with a new and sizable contract from the U.S. Navy. This is hardly the first contract it's secured with our nation's military, and it surely won't be the last.

Regardless, it's another feather in its cap and, hopefully, a sign of good things to come for both the firm and Pratt & Whitney, its aircraft engine subsidiary. Here's some detail about the deal, and how it'll affect RTX.

Recent findings suggest that on Wednesday evening, after the stock market closed for the Thanksgiving holiday, the Department of Defense (DoD) announced the award of the contract. Specifically, this is a nearly $2.53 billion award to Pratt & Whitney to deliver equipment and services for the F135 jet engine that powers the advanced F-35 Lightning II combat aircraft.

Per the DoD's press release on the award, it's an "undefinitized contract action with cost-plus-fixed-fee, cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost, and fixed-price-incentive-fee contract line items" for the plane.

Put in less bureaucratic language, the arrangement is for the RTX subsidiary to begin work on the project now, with the understanding that certain terms (such as final payment) are to be finalized later. This is a fairly standard type of defense company contract with the U.S. military, used when there is some urgency to a project, or simply a need to keep one running consistently and smoothly.

Many experts consider the F-35 Lightning II to be the most advanced multi-role fighter aircraft in our arsenal today. Given that, the Navy needs to ensure there are minimal gaps in the fleet's repairs and upkeep.

According to recent reports, the DoD added that the bulk of this work will be performed in corporate facilities or on military bases in this country. 14% is expected to be performed abroad, specifically in Italy, the U.K., Norway, the Netherlands, Japan, and Australia. The project is expected to be completed in November 2027. Defense was to obligate over $436 million upon contract award.

NYSE · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

In a recent development, this wasn't a particularly surprising development, which is likely why the investor reaction to the news was muted (RTX's stock was up only 0.5% in pre-market trading on Friday). Much of this is due to the long history both Pratt & Whitney and RTX's legacy Raytheon business have with the F-35 project, which stretches back to its beginnings in the 1990s.

It has been revealed that additionally, RTX is a sprawling defense conglomerate that pulled in nearly $89 billion in revenue last year. Of course, $2.5 billion-plus is more than just a drop in the bucket, but it's not going to suddenly transform the company in a meaningful way.

That said, the latest F-35 contract is sizable. The DoD's announcement was part of a broader press release detailing six recently-awarded contracts by branches of the U.S. military. RTX/Pratt & Whitney's was the largest and more than double No. 2, a $1.13 billion award from the Navy to Northrop Grumman (NOC +1.02%) for work on strategic communications aircraft. Outside of the Northrop Grumman contract, the others are in the tens of millions of dollars.

Recent findings suggest that the DoD is also significantly increasing its reliance on RTX, as the fresh contract's ceiling is around 58% higher than the preceding sustainment award RTX and its subsidiary received in late 2025. So, at the very least, I'd take this as a significant act of confidence and trust in the organization and its veteran engine specialist to perform mission-critical work during a time of increased global conflict. That's enough to keep me bullish on RTX's future.

Well, because sports betting seems to be everywhere these days, and I love sports. I bet you do, too. I've loved sports all my life. Increasingly, when I sit down to watch a football game, a baseball game, or a basketball game these days, I'm reminded that there's another game going on alongside the one that's on the field. Who's favored? What's the spread? What's the over-under? Who's going to score the next touchdown? Of course, would you like to put a little money on that? I find myself wondering whether we've reached a point where the business of betting on sports is beginning to crowd out, for some of us, the simple pleasure of watching sports. Just how substantial has this become? Well, according to the American Gaming Association in 2025, Americans placed nearly $167 billion in legal commercial sports bets. Yeah, that's “billion” with a B. How much did the sportsbooks keep after paying out their winners? Nearly $17 billion. That's about $0.10 of every dollar wagered. Think about that. $17 billion flowing net from sports bettors to the companies taking their bets in a single year. That's just sports betting.

Across casinos, online gambling, and sportsbooks, the American commercial gambling industry generated almost $79 billion in revenue last year. There's a newly introduced kid on the block: prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket among others. According to Pew Research Center, those two platforms alone recorded $53 billion in worldwide trading volume in July of this year, one month. Now, that's measured differently from sports betting, so we can't simply add those numbers together, yet much of that trading is now focused on sports. My point is simple. This is an enormous business, and it's getting bigger. Those billions flowing to the gambling operators, they're coming from somewhere, from where? From whom? Well, from the customers, their customers, from you. If you're their customer, that's your money they're taking hand over fist. Now, I want to make something clear up front. I believe sports betting should be legal. I've always believed that adults should be free to make our own decisions with our own money. That includes decisions that I might think are foolish. I've enjoyed friendly wagers myself over the years. There's nothing inherently wrong with two friends putting $5 on a game or the loser buying dinner. Yeah, I think there's an enormous difference between that and the industrial-scale business of persuading millions of people to bet and bet again and bet again.

According to recent reports, this week, I want to ask three questions. First, what does the math tell us? Second, what distinguishes sports betting from stock market investing? Third, a question that matters very much to me. I hope you, too, does it matter how we make our money? Let's start with a little math. I've often stated that investing in the stock market is a little like sailing. Imagine you and me sitting together in a sailboat, the wind pushing us forward. Well, that would be the stock market’s compounding positive returns. That wind is at our backs. When you're a stock market investor, the broad stock market consistently rises over time, even with, of course, the storm, and there will always be storms. Sometimes the wind blows right in our faces. Sometimes our boat gets tossed around. Over decades, though, investors have benefited from owning pieces of productive enterprises, companies that create goods and services, generate profits, and grow. Now, sports betting has a fundamentally different mathematical structure. Here's a simple example. Suppose you and I bet on opposite sides of a football game. We each have a 50% chance of winning. If we're just betting against each other, one of us wins, one of us loses. Between us, no wealth has been created.

Now introduce a sportsbook. A common arrangement requires you to risk $110 to win $100. So if you win, you make $100; if you lose, you're out $110. OK, so suppose you make 100 such bets, each one a genuine 50-50 proposition. You win 50 and lose 50. Well, on your 50 winners, you're going to make $5,000, and on your 50 losers, you're going to lose $5,500. Congratulations, you've gotten half your predictions right, and you've lost $500. You're a loser. That's not even including the time and the attention that you devoted to making those bets in the first place, which, by the way, might be just as expensive or even more so. Now, the rare skilled bettor may find favorable odds, and the precise mathematics are going to vary from wager to wager. The point is that the sportsbook’s margin — that middleman is creating a headwind that the typical bettor has to overcome in order just to break even.

Industry observers note that and this is where I want to pull a page from my book Rule Breaker Investing. Last September, my book Rule Breaker Investing was published. Here's what I wrote about sports betting, and I quote, "The key to principle number five is simple. They routinely have to take all-or-nothing propositions. They pay a middleman, the house, up to 10% commission and have to put down all their money before the race or the game starts. It's regrettable how easy and attractive sports betting is made to sound when it's such a losing play, day in and day out. I'm hoping this book reaches many and helps clarify for them why their money is so much better invested in the stock market. The market tends to rise over time, you and me in the sailboat, the wind at our backs. Sports betting, by its nature, is zero-sum, and your expected return is always negative. The handicaps are set very effectively, whether we’re talking about a 6.5-point favorite in basketball or seven-to-five odds at a horse track. One bettor will win, the other will lose, and the house will always take its cut. Over time, almost all consistent sports bettors lose money. What happens to those who consistently invest over time? The difference is immense.

Though sports betting is now widely legal in the U.S., that doesn't make it a smart bet. I've made friendly wagers with friends for decades, which can make watching games more fun and stressful. But I look askance at substantial-volume betting and especially its influence on the media coverage of sports I love. A booming gambling industry does not reflect my best vision for our future.     Should You Buy Nvidia Stock Before CEO Jensen Huang Testifies in Front of Congress on Dec. 1 and Dec. 3?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks.
    • Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching.
    • 1, Huang will testify before the U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:28PM EST.

    Jensen Huang may be back as CEO of Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), but the chip giant's worries are far from over, as regulators and lawmakers continue to investigate whether Nvidia breached export controls and whether Huang's relationship with a Singaporean data center executive may have posed national security risks.

    Huang and other Nvidia executives are set to testify before Congress next week on the above concerns, which the entire stock market will be watching.

    It has been revealed that on Dec. 1, Huang will testify before the U.S. House of Representatives' Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committee, and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. Nvidia's General Counsel Tim Teter will also testify before the same committees on Dec. 2. Both hearings will be private, with transcripts not expected to be published publicly for some time.

    Industry observers note that but on Dec. 3, Huang will testify at a live hearing before the U.S. Senate Banking Committee, an event that will be closely monitored by all investors. Should investors buy Nvidia stock before these hearings?

    While President Donald Trump has come out in support of Huang and claims to have played a role in his reinstatement, the hearings will help reveal how other lawmakers feel about Huang and what's going on with Nvidia.

    According to recent reports, "The market volatility and nervousness is centered on a number of issues that the Jensen soap opera has highlighted front and center," Yorkville Ives analyst and Managing Partner Dan Ives wrote in a recent research note, according to Business Insider. "Next week Jensen carries the weight of the entire tech sector and AI Revolution thesis when he marches into DC.".

    Huang's reinstatement as CEO led to a swift surge in the stock, but since then, shares have been pressured by lingering investor concerns about the company.

    Multiple reports suggest that a woman Huang had an affair with, named Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at the Singaporean data center firm MegaSpeed, may have facilitated a network that diverted advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.

    NASDAQ · As of 1:15 PM ET 11/27/26.

    It has been revealed that investors are trying to understand how much prior demand for Nvidia's chips, if any, may have been driven by similar sources. Since the scandal came to light, the U.S. Commerce Department has moved to close loopholes and tighten export controls that may have allowed Chinese firms to access Nvidia chips remotely.

    Industry observers note that the Commerce Department is now also requiring companies in select countries, such as Singapore and Indonesia, to obtain a license before transferring or reexporting advanced chips from U.S. companies.

    In his note, Ives said he believes the impact on revenue resulting from such export controls is "a containable 15% to 20% at most." Still, that's a significant amount, and while some of it is priced in, Nvidia stock could certainly face more pressure if it believed future demand wouldn't be as strong.

    Given that Wall Street analysts like Ives are already contemplating what would happen to Nvidia's revenue if increased export restrictions lower demand, or some sources of demand abroad are closed off, it's clear the market is pricing in at least some of the potential impact.

    Still, Wall Street consensus estimates expect Nvidia to earn $16.61 per share on an adjusted basis for its fiscal year 2028 ending in late January 2028. That means Nvidia trades at just 9x forward earnings, so the valuation is attractive.

    But as we've seen through this whole debacle, things can change in a hurry, so I would never tell investors to buy a stock based on a near-term event like a Congressional hearing.

    According to recent reports, with Nvidia trading at a cheap level, I think investors can purchase a position to hold long term. But I do not believe that the majority of a traditional stock portfolio should be concentrated in Nvidia or AI stocks, as much uncertainty remains.

    #154026. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (628 w)
    📖 Baca
    Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct.
    • According to recent reports, however, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive.
    • Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession strategy, makes it worse.

    According to recent reports, however, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a substantial haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

    Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

    Industry observers note that this prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

    Sources indicate that this lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

    By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

    #154021. Sovereign wealth funds are acting more like private equity giants — and inheriting their risks

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (941 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Sovereign wealth funds are acting more like private equity giants — and inheriting their risks

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • For decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf.
    • From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans.
    • "The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    For decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf. Increasingly, they are doing the dealmaking themselves.

    From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans.

    "The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry. This could bring more fundamental changes in the long term," Diego Lopez of Global SWF told CNBC.

    Limited partners, or LPs, typically commit capital to private equity funds, while general partners, or GPs, are responsible for sourcing deals and managing investments.

    Sovereign funds and state investment companies are increasingly taking on the GP role, Lopez stated, pointing to the establishment of their own private equity management platforms, such as Mubadala Capital and Singapore's Seviora.

    The shift is also reflected in the way some of the world's largest sovereign investors are approaching dealmaking.

    Recent findings suggest that "They originate transactions rather than waiting for them. They build platforms rather than buying single assets. They take control positions and operate what they own," PwC said in their latest report on sovereign wealth funds.

    "Whether you're a company, a general partner, or a government, you'll find that these institutions are no longer the limited partner you're raising money from; they're the principal sitting across the table.".

    Sources indicate that last year, Abu Dhabi's MGX, an investment vehicle established by state fund Mubadala in 2024, anchored the roughly $40 billion acquisition of Aligned Data Centers alongside BlackRock, Nvidia and Microsoft. A year earlier, a consortium led by Mubadala Capital acquired a 68% equity stake in alternative asset manager Fortress, which at the time managed more than $48 billion.

    Some sovereign funds are striking deals at a speed typically associated with large private equity firms, according to PwC.

    Singapore's GIC recorded 553 transactions between July 2023 and July 2026, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala 397 and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority 367, according to PwC's analysis of PitchBook data, which includes transactions by subsidiaries.

    The shift comes as sovereign wealth funds command unprecedented financial firepower. Their assets have surged about 59% over the past five years to $16.5 trillion, up from $10.4 trillion in 2022 and more than nine times the $1.8 trillion they managed in 2005, according to data provided to CNBC by research firm Global SWF which focuses on state-owned investors.

    PwC projects that sovereign wealth fund assets to reach $22.4 trillion by 2030.

    While sovereign funds' push into direct investing has been underway for years, a more challenging fundraising environment for PE firms and a resurgence in megadeals have recently accelerated the trend.

    The fundraising slowdown has tilted bargaining power toward large institutional investors, allowing them to negotiate more opportunities to invest directly alongside private equity managers, noted Kyle Walters of PitchBook.

    Sources indicate that A key attraction is the potential to save on fees. Co-investments typically carry little or no management fees and no carried interest, which is the share of investment profits that managers receive. Additionally, direct deals can eliminate external manager fees altogether.

    "For a large SWF writing major checks, the fee savings in dollar terms can be substantial," Walters said.

    In a recent development, sovereign funds also enjoy structural advantages over traditional buyout firms. Unlike conventional private equity funds, which operate within predetermined lifespans, sovereign investors can hold assets for decades, the experts highlighted.

    They can also deploy substantial sums from their own balance sheets without having to raise fresh capital, an advantage particularly valuable in capital-intensive sectors such as AI infrastructure and energy.

    But deep pockets and patient capital alone do not guarantee success.

    As sovereign wealth funds take controlling stakes in companies, they assume operational responsibilities traditionally borne by private equity managers, while potentially stretching their own capacity to source deals, conduct due diligence and manage complex assets, PwC cautioned.

    It has been revealed that "Building the required capability, the talent, the systems, and the governance is a slower process than committing the capital," PwC stated. The firm also flagged concentration risks as sovereign investors increasingly pile into similar investment themes, particularly AI, data centers and power infrastructure, leaving even geographically diversified portfolios vulnerable to the same underlying risks.

    Despite their growing ambitions, industry experts are skeptical that sovereign wealth funds will supplant established private equity managers.

    "This latest path these large LPs are paving is more of a partnership than a competition between GPs and LPs," Walters mentioned, noting that much of the increased activity is taking the form of co-investments.

    He pointed to the $55 billion take-private deal for video-game maker Electronic Arts confirmed last year, in which Saudi Arabia's PIF contributed significant capital, as an example of how both sides ae joining hands.

    Traditional buyout firms also retain an edge in sourcing deals and managing portfolio companies.

    "However, capital alone does not replace the specialist sourcing, operational expertise, and active ownership capabilities required to consistently create value, which experienced managers have built over time," mentioned Vincent Ng, managing director and co-head of Asia at Partners Group.

    Direct investing also raises concentration risks, while illiquidity could become a problem during crises when governments need access to capital, experts said.

    Rather than displacing traditional buyout firms, sovereign investors' growing ambitions could change the economics of private equity, forcing managers to become more flexible in how they work with their biggest clients.

    "This is likely to reshape the relationship between asset owners and managers, with more customized mandates, co-investments, and long-term partnerships," Ng said.

    Tech Report: Nvidia, Micron, and Sandisk Trade at Half the S&P 500’s Forward P/E. They Are All Genius Buys.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (747 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Comparing stocks to an index like the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) is a great way to assess their relative valuation.
    • Sources indicate that the same goes with being more expensive.
    • According to recent reports, three that are trading at massive discounts from the S&P 500 are Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), Sandisk (SNDK +15.96%), and Micron Technology (MU +7.60%).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Keithen Drury – Nov 27, 2026 at 2:38PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

    Comparing stocks to an index like the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.60%) is a great way to assess their relative valuation. For example, if a stock is trading at an earnings ratio that’s cheaper than the market average, there should be a good reason for that.

    Sources indicate that the same goes with being more expensive. What investors should often be looking for is stocks that are not valued marginally above or below the S&P 500, but under it by an amount significant enough to raise eyebrows when the business is assessed.

    According to recent reports, three that are trading at massive discounts from the S&P 500 are Nvidia (NVDA +0.80%), Sandisk (SNDK +15.96%), and Micron Technology (MU +7.60%). All three are posting monster growth figures, so if the reasons they trade at a discount don't hold water, then they are well worth buying at these prices.

    First, let's look at the forward price-to-earnings ratio of the S&P 500, which is currently 18. With Micron, Sandisk, and Nvidia's fiscal year not ending in the next 12 months exactly, there is a bit of a mismatch on end dates in this analysis. However, the offsetting periods aren’t so large that the difference really matters in this case.

    Both Sandisk and Micron are in their fiscal year 2027s right now, and each trades at a substantial discount to the market.

    SNDK PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts.

    It has been revealed that at just 3.6 times forward earnings, Micron looks like a bargain. Sandisk is even cheaper at 2.7 times forward earnings. That means these two are anywhere from five to six times cheaper than the S&P 500 is right now. That's a deep discount, but why do these two trade that low?

    Both companies make memory chips, which have two crucial use cases in AI: providing quick-access memory for computing units and long-term data storage. Demand for these chips from companies building data centers has exceeded the memory industry’s global production capacity. As a result, the memory market is now in a severely supply-constrained state.

    Industry observers note that simple economics states that when demand is high and supply is low, prices rise. That is exactly what has happened, and Micron and Sandisk have seen their revenues and profits skyrocket over the past year.

    Recent findings suggest that the low prices of these two stocks reflect the market’s bet that these conditions won't last and that a downturn in the memory market is inevitable. However, Micron's management team told investors during its most recent earnings call that it anticipates that memory market conditions will tighten even further in 2027 and 2028. So, these two companies have nothing to worry about in the short term, and that makes their stocks look like absolute bargains in the meantime.

    Industry observers note that the turmoil around GPU maker Nvidia has been hard to ignore if you're an investor. Furthermore, just because Jensen Huang is back in the CEO role doesn't mean that the manufacturer is in the clear. There are still concerns about whether some of Nvidia’s most powerful processors reached customers in China, despite U.S. trade rules that ban their export to that country.

    We'll learn more about what's going on with Nvidia when Huang testifies before Congress, but ongoing investigations could still reveal problems that impact the business.

    However, given that Huang was willing to return to the CEO role, I'd say the likelihood of anything too drastic happening is low; otherwise, he might have taken the opportunity to run for the hills.

    As a result of its troubles, Nvidia trades at 9.4 times 1-year forward earnings, a low price.

    NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

    That's about half the price of the S&P 500, but still more expensive than Sandisk or Micron. Regardless, I think all three are worthy buys at this price point, because they are all primed to benefit from the booming AI arms race.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The race for dominance in Formula 1 is no longer confined to the racetrack, with some of the world's biggest sportswear brands, including Nike, Adidas and Puma, vying for a piece of the action.
    • Sportswear sponsorship spending in F1 has surged 75% over two years and topped $200 million in 2026, according to Adam Lewis, a senior analyst at research firm Ampere Analysis.
    • Brands are competing for access to the sport's increasingly young and affluent fan base, while looking to capitalize on its growing influence in fashion and popular culture.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The race for dominance in Formula 1 is no longer confined to the racetrack, with some of the world's biggest sportswear brands, including Nike, Adidas and Puma, vying for a piece of the action.

    Sportswear sponsorship spending in F1 has surged 75% over two years and topped $200 million in 2026, according to Adam Lewis, a senior analyst at research firm Ampere Analysis.

    Brands are competing for access to the sport's increasingly young and affluent fan base, while looking to capitalize on its growing influence in fashion and popular culture.

    Sources indicate that nike gave fans a sneak preview of its F1 partnership in Las Vegas this month with a limited-edition collection sold during the Grand Prix. From 2027, Nike will supply F1 staff uniforms, a role Puma has held since 2024, and sell footwear and apparel under the championship's brand.

    In a recent development, other sportswear majors have taken a different approach. Adidas signed with Mercedes in 2025 and added Audi for its debut season this year, while Puma still has its longstanding deal with Ferrari, covering racewear and licensing for Ferrari-branded products.

    Unlike football leagues such as the English Premier League, where sportswear brands spread their budgets across numerous clubs, F1 has just 11 teams, limiting the number of apparel partnerships up for grabs.

    "F1, by contrast, is a closed market with only a handful of teams," Lewis mentioned, adding that the scarcity of deals makes brands more willing to pay higher prices as contracts come up for renewal.

    What makes F1 particularly attractive, however, is its growing influence.

    "For major sportswear and lifestyle brands, F1 has grown beyond motorsport, into a powerful, year-round pop-culture and storytelling platform," Joey Khong, global consumer trends manager at market research firm Mintel, told CNBC.

    F1 brings together fashion, music, luxury and celebrity culture with athletic performance and technological innovation, offering brands multiple avenues to engage with consumers, Khong said.

    Team apparel has also crossed over into everyday streetwear, with social media amplifying the visibility of what drivers and team members wear off the track.

    Some 34% of people who engage with F1 do so through social media, while 22% engage through online content, according to Lewis.

    That constant stream of content has turned team apparel into what Lewis described as a "living billboard" for sportswear brands.

    Equally key is who is watching.

    Nearly a third of F1 fans are now under the age of 35, with that share rising 18% since 2023, according to Lewis. Meanwhile, 45% of F1 fans fall into the two highest-earning socioeconomic groups, compared with 36% of the general population.

    For sportswear brands, F1 offers a way to build loyalty among younger, affluent consumers.

    Asia-Pacific has been a key driver of F1's fan growth, helping deliver a larger audience for its commercial partners, analysts said.

    Markets across the region have gained more than 25 million F1 fans since 2023, up 36%, according to Ampere Analysis. That outpaced growth in other markets by 11 percentage points and accounted for 84% of overall fan growth.

    That offers sportswear brands a growing audience to engage with in a region where F1 already races in Melbourne, Suzuka, Shanghai and Singapore.

    Research also points to why that engagement could resonate. In a 2026 Mintel survey, 29% of respondents in China said sporting events would prompt them to pay attention to or try related brands, rising to 37% in households earning at least 24,000 yuan ($3,600) a month.

    Fans are spending more on F1 merchandise than ever before.

    F1 merchandise sales have grown by almost 200% since 2017, according to Fanatics, the sport's e-commerce partner, cited in a License Global report.

    Retail sales of F1-licensed consumer products also rose 44% in 2024, one of the fastest growth rates among the sports properties tracked.

    The appeal may stretch beyond race-branded gear. F1 fans were 29% more likely than the average consumer to say they planned to buy sports apparel in the next year and 27% more likely to say the same about non-sports apparel, according to Ampere's consumer research.

    Mintel's Khong stated F1 merchandise alone is unlikely to move the needle quickly for sports apparel giants the size of Nike or Adidas.

    Instead, the bigger potential payoff could come from the partnership boosting demand across the brand's everyday product lines outside F1-specific collaborations or the sport's licensed merchandise.

    "There is a route to revenue growth, but being associated with the sport is only the starting point," Khong remarked.
