    Latest Update: Pfizer's 6% Yield vs. AbbVie's 53-Year Dividend Streak: Which Stock Is the Better Buy?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:05PM EST.
    • AbbVie's (ABBV -0.88%) 2.3% dividend yield pales in comparison to Pfizer's (PFE +0.21%) 6%.
    • In a recent development, one of the major positives of AbbVie as an investment is that it is a Dividend King.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 27, 2026 at 3:05PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than AbbVie ›.

    AbbVie's (ABBV -0.88%) 2.3% dividend yield pales in comparison to Pfizer's (PFE +0.21%) 6%. But it is important to recognize that the average drug organization's yield is only 1.3% and the broader market's yield is just 1%, so AbbVie's yield isn't exactly small. Here's why conservative dividend investors wouldn't be making a mistake by buying AbbVie, but if you can handle a little uncertainty, Pfizer's much higher yield may end up being the better option.

    In a recent development, one of the major positives of AbbVie as an investment is that it is a Dividend King. That means that the organization has increased its dividend annually for 50+ consecutive years (53 to be specific), which is not something that happens by accident. It requires a strong business model that is executed well in both good and bad markets. The only problem here is that AbbVie hasn't actually existed for 50 years. It was created in 2013 when it was spun off from Abbott Laboratories (ABT +0.07%). It retained Abbott's dividend record and then, to AbbVie's credit, continued to raise its dividend each year.

    Still, it probably isn't appropriate to give AbbVie full credit for its Dividend King status. You should pay extra attention to its actual business, which is well-run and fairly well-positioned. It has strong positions in immunology and oncology. Meanwhile, the drug maker's aesthetics business doesn't face the same patent risks as other drug niches because brand names are important differentiators. As a business, it is highly desirable.

    In a recent development, there's just one small problem: the stock isn't cheap. Its price-to-sales ratio is 7.9x compared to a five-year average of 5.4x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 50x compared to a five-year average of 41x. You are paying full fair, if not more, for the stock's above-average yield.

    NYSE · As of 1:00 PM ET 11/27/26.

    That's where Pfizer starts to look relatively attractive. Not only is its dividend yield likely to be highly attractive to income seekers, but the stock is also much cheaper than AbbVie. Pfizer's 2.5x P/S ratio is in line with its five-year average and far lower than AbbVie's 7.9x. Pfizer's P/E ratio is 40x, which is biased higher by one-time charges and still lower than AbbVie's 50x. If you use the $3.00 per share midpoint of Pfizer's 2026 adjusted earnings guidance, the P/E is around 10x. That's below the stock's nearly 14x five-year average.

    It has been revealed that A significant yield from a cheap stock will likely have more appeal than a smaller yield from an expensive stock for most investors. But there are challenges to consider, most notably Pfizer's upcoming patent expirations in 2028 (Eliquis) and 2031 (Vyndamax). Those are big deals and will likely result in a substantial decline in revenues and earnings. The thing is, patent expirations are entirely normal in the pharmaceutical sector. Pfizer is working hard to develop new drugs to offset the hit, but sometimes the timing doesn't perfectly align.

    NYSE · As of 1:01 PM ET 11/27/26.

    Still, given the firm's strong history, which dates back to the mid-1800s, it seems highly likely that it will manage this patent expiration cycle, just as it has many times before. As for the dividend, the company is publicly supportive of it and continues to tell investors that its long-term goal is to grow the payment. And even if there were a 50% dividend cut, which seems like a reasonable worst-case scenario, the yield would still be higher than AbbVie's 2.3%.

    Industry observers note that if you are a risk-averse investor who simply can't tolerate any kind of uncertainty, AbbVie is a perfectly fine, though perhaps expensive, stock to buy. However, Pfizer's higher yield and more attractive valuation will probably make it a better option, assuming you believe it can muddle through its patent-expiration issues, as it has many times before. Indeed, the risk-versus-reward balance is likely tilted toward reward for long-term dividend investors.

    #154007. Industry News: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1165 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Latin America has the copper and energy the AI build-out needs. Infrastructure is the test

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.
    • But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.
    • "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Latin America’s copper, energy and mineral resources could play a growing role in supplying the global artificial-intelligence build-out, as data centers and electrification drive demand for power and raw materials.

    But for investors, it's less about whether Latin America has the resources than whether governments can turn them into viable projects.

    "We are going through an acceleration in energy demand growth. We need every possible energy source available," Michele Della Vigna, head of natural resources research for Goldman Sachs, told CNBC. "Ultimately, what drives economic growth is energy," he added.

    According to recent reports, ben Kumar, head of strategy for wealth, investment and public policy at 7IM, suggested Latin America could benefit, given the physical materials needed for AI equipment and data centers. "We are right now neutral in the short term, but if the materials and mining cycle continues, we could see this moving to positive in a few months," he remarked.

    According to recent reports, the investment case varies across the region. Chile has copper; Argentina is expanding oil and gas exports; and Brazil has abundant renewable power and significant rare earth reserves.

    Industry observers note that chile's copper sector illustrates both the supply potential and the constraints to expanding supply. Copper production fell 8.5% in the first nine months of 2026, according to the state copper commission Cochilco, as lower ore grades, maintenance, and operational disruptions constrained supply.

    In a recent development, but demand for refined copper is set to grow 1.6% this year and 2% next year, according to the International Copper Study Group. Supply is struggling to keep pace with demand from expanding electricity grids.

    Chile's copper commission has raised its 2027 price forecast to $5.95 a pound, from $5.10. Codelco, the state-owned copper producer, may also have scope to increase supply, including through proposed public-private partnerships.

    Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, sees demand continuing to grow. "As countries expand electricity grids, they need more copper regardless of which power source they choose," he said.

    Industry observers note that the scale of the opportunity will depend in part on how rapidly energy demand grows. Goldman Sachs forecasts that global power demand for data centers will grow by 170% by 2030. The IEA projected in April that global data center electricity consumption would rise from 485 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030.

    Industry observers note that the investment case also depends on whether the region can capture more value from the resources it produces. Latin America and the Caribbean refined only 26% of the copper they mined in 2025, according to the IEA.

    "Cautious optimism is justified and there will be massive critical mineral demand," said Monica de Bolle, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.

    "But improving refining capacity will be crucial to capture more of that value," she added.

    Some projects have already secured financing. Chilean explorer Marimaca Copper Corp selected a preferred lender for a $400 million debt facility to build a mine on Oct. 28. The funding will go towards developing an open-pit mine in the north of Chile that will produce 50,000 metric tons of refined copper annually. Production is expected from 2029.

    Argentina shows the other side of the opportunity: strong oil and gas resources, but insufficient infrastructure to get more production to global markets.

    According to recent reports, "I see an opportunity in the infrastructure that gets Argentine oil and gas to market. A producer in Vaca Muerta can have excellent wells and still struggle to expand exports without pipeline capacity and access to ports.

    It has been revealed that that gives investors a reason to look at transport and export infrastructure alongside production," Rafael Ch, partner and senior analyst for Latin America and emerging markets at Signum Global Advisors, added. Vaca Muerta is Argentina's vast shale basin.

    Argentina is also attracting investment in drilling and export infrastructure. International capital markets have reopened to investment in drilling and pipelines in Argentina. That investment has already driven the build-out of a pipeline and port. Argentina will then be able to export far more crude oil. Chevron and American oil tycoon Harold Hamm have also increased their investments in Argentina.

    Industry observers note that brazil's case rests partly on its renewable-heavy power mix. About 89% of the country's electricity was generated from renewable sources in 2025, according to the country's Ministry of Mines and Energy.

    "That puts Brazil in a strong position to benefit as AI and data centers drive up demand," Stephanie Link, chief investment strategist and portfolio manager at Hightower Advisors, told CNBC.

    But while Brazil has the world's second-largest reported rare-earth reserves, its estimated mine production is far smaller than China's. USGS estimates put Brazil's output at 2,000 metric tons in 2025, compared with China's 270,000 metric tons. Brazil's reserves are estimated at 11 million metric tons by the USGS, second only to China's 44 million metric tons.

    For investors, the gap between Brazil's vast reserves and limited current production is both the opportunity and the execution risk.

    For investors, the policy question is whether governments can make projects viable and keep them on track.

    Luis Costa, Citi's global head of emerging markets strategy, said governments need to offer incentives, particularly in the early stages of projects, because infrastructure lags the region's resource wealth. He also stressed that support must last: infrastructure projects can take several years to develop.

    The World Bank's Latin America and the Caribbean Economic Patch for 2026 projects growth for the region of 2.2%, and highlights the "restricted fiscal space, sticky inflation and high borrowing costs.".

    "The economic policy and fiscal policy needs to get in line as markets are globally becoming more sensitive to fiscal stories," said Costa.

    Brazil will need to establish fiscal credibility to attract investment, particularly if higher public spending puts additional pressure on debt and borrowing costs. "If investors doubt the government can stabilize public debt, companies' long-term financing costs could stay high even as the central bank lowers its policy rate," Ch added.

    Industry observers note that with Argentina set for national elections in October 2027, political continuity will also matter for energy investment. "A return to tighter currency controls or persistent deficits would make companies more likely to delay projects, even in an oil field with attractive economics," stated Ch.

    Pro-business President Javier Milei faces a tight race for re-election, though a change in leadership would not necessarily undermine medium- to long-term investment.

    "There is also the possibility of a pragmatic Peronist ticket emerging, which markets would be satisfied with," stated Nicolas Jaquier, emerging-market fixed-income portfolio manager at Ninety One.

    For those governing across Latin America, policies to unlock its wealth of resources will be key for it to emerge as a winner from the AI demand boom.

    "Supply chain security is becoming more and more relevant, and if commodities take off Latin America can be a clear and obvious winner," remarked Kumar.

    #154004. Breaking: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

    Breaking: Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.
    • Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.
    • The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

    Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

    The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

    The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

    Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

    Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

    After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

    They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

    Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

    We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the organization's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

    It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

    As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

    On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

    Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

    If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

    The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance.".

    The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

    Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks latest CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

    In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to rapidly disclose any sales.

    Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

    That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

    It has been revealed that the case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

    Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

    Industry observers note that in the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

    All those numbers exclude the manufacturer's buybacks of its own stock.

    In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway indicates it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

    Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

    It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

    In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

    Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

    Some links may require a subscription:.

    Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most key ideas.

    Recent findings suggest that WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

    You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

    In a recent development, two of the — well, all of the key ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

    One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

    And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

    And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that claims it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds.".

    Lower interest rates narrowed the financial margin, or net yield on earning assets, to 14.4%. Management aims to rebuild sustainable profitability through higher transaction volumes and fee growth, targeting a 15% return on equity, a measure of net income relative to shareholder equity, by 2028.

    Industry observers note that macroeconomic stabilization continues to lower inflation rates. Management expects real loan growth between 5% and 10% next year, supported by recovering consumer demand and a lower cost of risk, which measures expected credit losses against total loans.

    According to recent reports, capital strength remains high, with computable capital exceeding regulatory minimums by 4.8 trillion Argentine pesos. A diversified business model across banking, asset management, and insurance positions the bank to capture growth as credit markets normalize.

    • Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.
    • Industry observers note that it comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov.
    • It has been revealed that chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.

    Industry observers note that it comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.

    It has been revealed that chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.

    According to recent reports, the interim final rule was declared by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.

    Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.

    It has been revealed that the new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.

    Sources indicate that nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for latest buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people mentioned it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.

    According to recent reports, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes.".

    "Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said.

    U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.

    According to recent reports, separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

    #153988. Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1624 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

    Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1624 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.
    • He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit on Thursday.
    • De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.

    He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit on Thursday. The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.

    De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.

    He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.

    Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.

    Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.

    It has been revealed that de Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.

    Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.

    Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.

    Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.

    That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.

    De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.

    "It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. However, his monetary policy views may well be regime-dependent," Christian Kopf, head of fixed income and foreign exchange at Union Investment, said in emailed comments.

    "We are now clearly in a higher-inflation regime, with core inflation in the euro area expected to remain above the ECB's target through 2029.".

    Kopf added that de Cos was the candidate with the "strongest technical understanding of monetary policy and central banking," which he remarked was crucial at a time when the world is "witnessing an assault on central bank independence, not only in the United States but also in countries such as Japan.".

    "By appointing a career technocrat such as Hernández de Cos as ECB President, the European Council would send a strong signal that Europe will not waver in its commitment to price stability and that the euro will remain a hard currency," Kopf said.

    Industry observers note that spain's de Cos as president, Germany's Brunnermeier as chief economist and France's Boone as head of market operations represent a "carefully crafted package deal," Kopf also noted, because it balances representation from northern and southern European countries. The result was partially due to the knock-on effects of the German government pushing hard for the chief economist position, he said.

    Along with a desire among politicians for influence, a north-south balance is seen as important as the northern countries are seen as leaning more hawkish — more inclined to opt for rate hikes and restrictive policy to tame inflation — while southern are perceived as more dovish.

    John Orchard, chairman of the Digital Monetary Institute at think tank OMFIF, said that as a "central banker's central banker," de Cos had "managed to earn respect from typically hawkish northern observers.".

    Another supportive factor of de Cos's candidacy was the stellar growth rate of many of those southern economies in recent years.

    Once the "sick men" of the euro area's 2010s sovereign debt crisis, Portugal, Italy, Spain and Greece have become some of the bloc's strongest growth drivers in recent years.

    Factors such as strong tourism, relative political stability, increased foreign investment and strengthening public finances have boosted southern economies. Meanwhile, the euro zone's traditional powerhouse Germany has stuttered amid soaring industrial costs and a struggling autos market.

    Orchard stated that some believed that Lagarde's presidency had ushered in an "esprit de corps" at the ECB, with policymakers focused on the interests of the whole European economy.

    That would, in theory, reduce the importance of nationality among leadership and of traditional notions of hawkish northern nations and dovish southern ones. However, Orchard also noted the recurrent theme of national representation in the recent debate and the perception of Knot as a hawkish choice.

    Diverging performance is a core challenge for any leader of the ECB, which must set monetary policy for 21 economies all growing at different speeds and with their own domestic priorities and inflationary pressures.

    But it has become particularly pressing this year as the bloc's second-biggest economy, France, is teetering on the edge of its own potential debt crisis.

    Moves in French markets and whether the ECB needs to take more extreme measures beyond continuing to urge fiscal discipline will remain in focus for de Cos.

    The ECB Executive Board's view of what measures could be taken to prevent market disorder and under what conditions was a key topic under discussion when choosing who should fill the roles, according to insiders.

    Despite political efforts to pass a budget that will reduce its budget deficit to around 5% of GDP, investors have been driving up French borrowing costs on concerns over its mounting public debt-to-GDP ratio, high budget deficit and contracting economy.

    Risks are being compounded by political uncertainty ahead of France's presidential election in April, which is stymying business activity and raising wider questions about EU unity as far-right and far-left candidates pull ahead.

    Rising French yields and the widening spread in France's borrowing costs over Germany's have led to speculation over whether the ECB might need to deploy tools such as liquidity injections or its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument to protect other countries from contagion and support the euro.

    This would be politically controversial unless France agreed to stringent fiscal discipline measures akin to those that southern nations signed up to during the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which could be complicated if far-right presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, who has a combative relationship with EU institutions, wins.

    Ken Egan, head of European sovereigns at ratings agency KBRA, stated fragmentation was always a challenge for the ECB, which does not want to see divergent financing conditions and high sovereign spreads across the bloc.

    However, he noted that in the case of France he believed we were "some way from having a serious conversation about ECB intervention.".

    "If anything, sovereign spreads have pulled back a bit and tightened, and some measures of market liquidity have also improved in recent weeks," he said by email.

    "That doesn't mean the underlying risks have disappeared, but I think it's important to distinguish between periods of market volatility and a more fundamental breakdown in monetary policy transmission.".

    De Cos also takes up the mantle as Europe faces yet another surge in price pressures.

    It has been revealed that euro area inflation rose to 4% in October, its highest level in more than three years. Energy was the biggest contributor, as the Iran war drives up oil and gas prices and tightens the supply of refined fuels.

    That leaves the central bank facing a difficult policy balance, preventing higher energy costs from spreading into wages and wider prices while avoiding unnecessary damage to growth.

    De Cos will inherit major supranational projects, including plans for a digital euro and Europe's long-delayed capital-markets integration. In a recent speech, Lagarde warned that each year without capital markets integration meant "more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding.".

    France is not the only euro area country heading for a pivotal election next year, with votes in Finland, Greece, Italy, Estonia, Slovakia and Slovenia also expected, adding to the politically uncertain climate.

    It is also not the only country grappling with higher government borrowing costs, public debt and a struggle to find fiscal headroom, a growing problem among many developed countries.

    Recent findings suggest that the ECB's Financial Stability Review meanwhile warned this month of mounting risks from European investors' growing exposure to the U.S. economy, and equity and credit markets' vulnerability to AI.

    Outgoing head Lagarde, meanwhile, told the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt this month that her biggest concern was now cyber threats, an area she said policymakers had not paid enough attention.

    Recent findings suggest that "The one [worry] that keeps me awake, and many of you awake ​as well ... ​is ⁠AI applied together with cyber threat," she said.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 27, 2026 at 3:38PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than GoDaddy ›.

    Picture a small-town baker who needs a way for customers to find her shop, pay for her croissants, and order for pickup without needing a degree in computer science. She heads to the web, types in a name, and clicks buy. For more than 20 million customers, that first step happens on GoDaddy (GDDY -1.97%).

    In a recent development, as a provider of domain registration, hosting, and commerce tools for entrepreneurs, the company acts as the digital storefront for the micro-business economy. The stock trades at $102.09 as of November 19, 2026, down roughly 18% over the past year despite recent operational gains.

    In a recent development, our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns GoDaddy an overall Superscore of 81 out of 100, placing it in the Strong category. The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a tech giant's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39).

    This score places GoDaddy in the Top ~9% of all companies we score, ahead of roughly 91 out of every 100 companies we track. The Superscore serves as one data-driven signal to help you weigh the firm's business model against your own research before doing further work.

    It has been revealed that although a mature tech company, the rise of artificial intelligence has given GoDaddy novel opportunities. Its Airo AI platform is becoming its flagship product, as the fresh solution hit an annualized bookings run rate of over $100 million in the third quarter, and began contributing to bookings growth.

    According to recent reports, the manufacturer's historically robust retention rate above 85% is boosted by the fact over half its customers pay for at least two products, adding to revenue growth. For those who adopt Airo, 70% have at least two paid products, suggesting its shift to the fresh solution is contributing to even stronger sales expansion.

    GoDaddy management is also adept at maintaining strong financials. It produced free cash flow of $480.8 million in Q3, representing a 9% year-over-year increase, while its balance sheet sported $1.1 billion in cash and equivalents. This gives the company flexibility to perform share repurchases while investing in new opportunities.

    Recent findings suggest that these factors position the tech giant for growth in the coming years. Combined with a reasonable trailing P/E of 14.1, well below the 24.4 multiple shares were at in Q3 of 2025, make the company a compelling stock to consider buying now.
